extracted.intended_audience: general readers and fans of British television/comedy
extracted.subtask_short: documenting a British stand-up TV series
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting production and evaluative features of a British stand-up comedy television series (format, recurring elements, critical reception) as exemplified by Stewart Lee's Comedy Vehicle. Useful for understanding what the show consists of and what critics identified as its qualities and flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live club-recorded stand-up performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The bulk of the show is a Stewart Lee stand-up comedy performance, recorded live at the Mildmay Club in Stoke Newington with a club audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually two episodes were recorded per evening; the live club setting and audience interaction are core to the programme's format and performance energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Themed episode structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Each episode has a theme, which Lee performs with his material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes are united by a theme (e.g., 'Television', 'Religion', 'Charity'), shaping the set and providing structural unity for the stand-up and accompanying segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sketches or short films to punctuate stand-up
rubrics_metrics.description: The stand-up is punctuated with sketches (series 1) usually performed by others; from series 2 the sketches were removed in favour of a short film at the end of each episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early series used sketches performed by Kevin Eldon, Paul Putner and others; later series replaced sketches with a short film closing the episode—this is a deliberate production choice affecting tone and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile interrogator/meta-interview segments
rubrics_metrics.description: An element of the programme is the 'hostile interrogator' in a darkened room, who quizzes Lee about his approach to stand-up comedy and his attitudes toward his audience and the comedy industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Played by Armando Iannucci (series 2) and Chris Morris (series 3 & 4); in Series 1 these segments were Red Button/DVD extras but were integrated into the main programme from Series 2—serves as meta-commentary and framing device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration and placement of bonus/interrogator content
rubrics_metrics.description: In Series 1 the interrogator segments were not included in the main programme, accessed instead via the BBC Red Button and included on the DVD releases as bonus features; the interrogator segments were integrated into the main body of the show by Series 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement (main programme vs. bonus content) affects audience experience and the prominence of meta-commentary; integration signals centrality to the show's concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening/closing tone-setting elements (theme tune vs cold open)
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening theme tune to Series 1 is 'Tom Hark'; from Series 2 there is a cold open and no theme tune or title card.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice between theme tune and cold open contributes to the show's tonal shift and viewer expectations; producers can adjust opening elements to change pacing and formality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative use of previously performed material
rubrics_metrics.description: Some material in episodes first appeared in earlier stand-up shows (e.g., 'Some material in this episode first appeared in 41st Best Stand-up Ever'; routines developed from Lee's 2005 show 90s Comedian).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reusing and developing material across live shows and TV allows refinement; episodes may contain developed versions of earlier routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative writing contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Several lines in series were written by other comedians (e.g., Bridget Christie, Simon Munnery, Tim Richardson); some jokes in episodes were written by named contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Lee is creator and writer, occasional contributions from other writers/comics are part of the creative process and can be credited in episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience control and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Chris Morris quizzes him on his audience control; one episode includes an ad-libbed section when an audience member leaves the room at an inopportune time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective management of a live audience (control, handling interruptions, ad-libbing) is presented as an important aspect of the performance and is explicitly examined within the programme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan/bone-dry delivery and skeptical tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics described Lee as 'the master of deadpan stand-up' with 'bone-dry, spot-on scepticism' that distinguished him from more perky or aggressive panel-show styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical praise highlights a dry, intellectual delivery and sceptical outlook as hallmarks of the show's comedic voice; this is a stylistic criterion audiences and critics used to evaluate the programme positively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligent, thought-provoking comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times called the series 'the most intelligent half hour of stand-up you will see on television this year'; others said 'It's comedy that makes you stop and think.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being intellectually rigorous and prompting reflection are presented as measures of the programme's quality rather than just chasing laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incisive, wide-ranging commentary to avoid self-indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellen Jones wrote that 'this comedy about comedy would be unforgivably self-indulgent if Lee wasn't just as incisive on every other facet of modern life as he is on his own comedic genius.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical approval ties avoidance of self-indulgence to the comedian's ability to be incisive across topics; breadth and sharpness of commentary are virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone as potential negative: smug condescension
rubrics_metrics.description: One negative review stated: 'His whole tone is one of complete, smug condescension.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics identified an anti-pattern where the performer's tone can be perceived as condescending; this is a cautionary evaluative criterion indicating when the style may alienate viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of topical and cultural references
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes explore subjects via references to cultural figures and events (e.g., references to Russell Brand, Dan Brown, The March of the Penguins, Woolworths, the European migrant crisis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent topical/cultural allusions structure jokes and themes; their selection and treatment contribute to topical relevance and comedic effect.
